description_full: Texas Capital Bancshares, Inc. operates as the bank holding company for Texas Capital Bank, is a full-service financial services firm that delivers customized solutions to businesses, entrepreneurs, and individual customers. The company offers commercial banking; consumer banking; investment banking solutions, including capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, and syndicated finance, as well as financial sponsor coverage, capital solutions, and institutional services; and wealth management services, such as investment management, financial planning, lockbox and insurance, securities-based lending, estate planning, and business succession, as well as philanthropic, trustee and executor, custom credit, and depository services. It also provides deposit accounts, analyzed accounts, commercial card, SBA and business loans, packaged solutions, and merchant services; liquidity and investments, working capital, international trade and payment, and treasury and credit products; and commercial real estate, homebuilder and community, and mortgage finance. In addition, the company offers payables and receivables management; online and mobile banking; term loans and lines of credit, equipment finance and lease, acquisition finance, and asset-based lending; private wealth advisory solutions; and checking and savings accounts, debit and credit cards, and certificates of deposit, as well as ETF and funds management services. Further, it provides financial institution money market accounts and loan syndication products; commercial loans for financing for working capital, organic growth, and acquisitions; real estate term and construction loans; mortgage warehouse lending services; treasury management, trust, and advisory and escrow services; and letters of credit. The company operates in Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, and San Antonio metropolitan areas of Texas, as well as in California and New York. The company was incorporated in 1996 and is headquartered in Dallas, Texas.

financial_summary: Texas Capital Bancshares, Inc. is a mid-cap financial services business with a $4.4B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $348M in free cash flow — roughly 28 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.09× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 5.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.3) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Elevated short interest (14.1% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Revenue growth lags most Financial Services peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Credit cycles and regulatory capital — losses accumulate invisibly in good years and appear all at once, and the time to worry is when underwriting standards are loosest.
Interest rate regime shifts — a rapid move in rates can invert the yield curve, crush bond portfolios, and trigger deposit flight simultaneously.

sector_tailwinds: Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 34% operating margin runs 5pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.33x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+21.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 7% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.31 vs 5y 0.79), so read it loosely.
About $45.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 67% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 69% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 10% below its DCF fair value of $112, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 2%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $85.73 to $148 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 2% above its 10-year median.
The 13 covering analysts target $106 on average, 5% above the price.
The price implies 3.8% annual cash-flow growth, 1pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.84).
It converts 28% of revenue into free cash flow.
It earns a 9% return on equity.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.8% over 3 years, 3.6% over 5 years and 7.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 13.0% on average.
Analysts expect 7.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 4 purchases and 4 sales over the past year, net $9.9M sold.
It returns 5.0% a year to shareholders (4.2% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 3.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 14.1% of the float, 8.5 days to cover.
people: With about 1,785 employees, each generates about $704K of revenue, 1.4x the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 8.7% a year.
That works out to $195K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.4M (5x revenue per employee).
